refutations.argument: The rule is worded for 'a multiplayer match', so it covers team games. CR 104.2c says a player who lost earlier can be on the team that wins, and then wins the game. In a team game the 'player who lost first' can therefore be a winner of the previous game. The stipulation makes that winner 'the loser of the previous game' who chooses who goes first, which contradicts 103.1: the chooser must be a loser, and a player who won the game is not one. The rule is overbroad and gives a wrong answer in a situation the official sources settle.

source.excerpt: Each player on the winning team wins the game, even if one or more of those players had previously lost that game.

steps.conclusion: In a team game, a player who lost first can still be a winner of that game.

source.excerpt: the loser of the previous game chooses who takes the first turn

steps.conclusion: 103.1 gives the choice to a loser, so C3, which gives it to 'the player who lost first' even when that player won the game under S1, conflicts with 103.1.

refutations.argument: The rule applies to every multiplayer match of several games, with no carve-out. In an Archenemy game CR 103.1b says the usual methods are not used and the archenemy takes the first turn. Under the stipulation, if two non-archenemy players lost the previous game, the player who lost first would choose who takes the first turn, so a Archenemy match gives a different starting player from the one 103.1b fixes.

source.excerpt: Rather, the archenemy takes the first turn.

steps.conclusion: In an Archenemy game the archenemy takes the first turn and no loser chooses.

source.excerpt: In an Archenemy game, these methods

steps.conclusion: The method in C3 is one of 103.1's methods and 103.1b excludes it in an Archenemy game, so the rule as worded in 'applies_when' (any multiplayer match) gives an answer the CR contradicts.

refutations.argument: The rule and its applies_when cover both 'more than one player lost' and 'the previous game was a draw' without saying which governs when both are true. CR 104.4a makes a game a draw if all remaining players lose simultaneously, and players who left earlier have lost. In a three-player game where A loses first and then B and C lose together, the stipulation names A as the chooser, while 103.1's draw sentence gives the choice to whoever chose in that game. The case gives no order between the two, so the rule yields two answers for the same game.

source.excerpt: If all the players remaining in a game lose simultaneously, the game is a draw.

steps.conclusion: A game in which one player lost earlier and the rest then lose together is a draw, and also one that more than one player lost.

source.excerpt: If the previous game was a draw, the player who made the choice in that game makes the choice in this game.

steps.conclusion: 103.1 gives the choice to the previous chooser in a draw, while C3 gives it to the first loser; the rule does not say which applies.

refutations.argument: The stipulation does not say who the first loser is when players lose at the same time, and that is the ordinary case. CR 704.3 has the game perform all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event, so life-total, poison and Commander-damage losses at one check are simultaneous. The tie-break the user gave (the tied players decide between themselves, else random) is in their confirm words, not in the case, so C3 and the 'rule' do not contain it. As worded, the rule gives no chooser whenever two players lose at the same check.

source.excerpt: performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event

steps.conclusion: Two players can lose at the same state-based action check, so neither 'lost first', and C3 names no chooser.
